variants.name: Intrinsic monitors (synchronized interface methods)
variants.idiom_name: public synchronized methods + private unsynchronized implementation methods
variants.implementation_notes: Oracle's tutorial states that intrinsic locks are reentrant - a thread can acquire a lock it already owns - so a Java component that calls its own synchronized methods does not self-deadlock; the split then delivers the minimal-locking-overhead half of the pattern, keeping the hold count at 1 and the critical section explicit. Mark the public methods synchronized (or wrap them in synchronized (lock) on a dedicated final object) and let them forward to private unsynchronized methods that assume the monitor is held. Java's concurrent collections and atomics replace the need entirely in many components; keep the split where several mutations must stay atomic within one public call, and move to an explicit ReentrantLock when the boundary needs tryLock, timeouts or interruptibility.
pitfalls: The monitor is reentrant, so a violation does not deadlock - it only raises the hold count, which makes the mistake invisible and lets the split decay unnoticed.
Locking on this or on a Class object exposes the monitor to collaborators; prefer a dedicated private final lock object.
Callbacks, listener dispatch and blocking I/O inside the synchronized block hold the monitor across foreign code - the classic lock-order-inversion and long-hold-time source.
Virtual threads pin their carrier thread inside synchronized blocks, so blocking there destroys the scalability the split is supposed to protect.

variants.name: Explicit ReentrantLock boundary
variants.idiom_name: lock.lock()/unlock() in finally + private implementation methods
variants.implementation_notes: ReentrantLock moves the boundary from a language keyword to explicit code: the public method calls lock(), forwards to the private implementation method inside a try block and unlocks in finally. Reentrancy and hold counts are documented properties of the class, and tryLock/tryLock(timeout)/lockInterruptibly give the boundary acquisition semantics the intrinsic monitor cannot express, so this variant is the choice when the component must bound how long it waits for its own lock, must be interruptible, or wants fair ordering - the split itself is unchanged, the private methods still never take the lock.
pitfalls: A missing finally leaks the lock permanently; unlike C#'s lock statement nothing in the compiler enforces it.
unlock() from a non-owner throws IllegalMonitorStateException; if lockInterruptibly or tryLock failed, do not unlock in finally.
Reentrancy still hides nested acquisition (the hold count rises), and the same lock must not be mixed with synchronized blocks on the same object.
